name: Liam Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the health and social care reporter at the regional newsroom of the public broadcaster, so I write for the website and do short pieces for the morning radio show. A normal day starts at eight with the editorial meeting, then I'm usually ringing hospital press offices, or out at a care home or a GP surgery talking to people. The bit I love is the people on waiting lists, the ones who've been told eighteen months for a hip, because their stories actually move the health board.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Radio, honestly. I'm still nervous on air, and Martin, my editor, keeps telling me to slow down and stop saying um. Also Mondays, which are mostly rewriting press releases from the health board into something readable. I use an AI tool now and then to tidy up interview transcripts, but that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds fine to me, to be honest. Transcripts get a bit quicker and the rest stays the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, newsrooms got sold a lot of hype. I'd probably say it on the team chat with a bit of a told-you-so. Reporting is mostly ringing people and turning up, and you can't automate turning up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job is about as safe as a junior job gets. The public broadcaster's budget is tight but our regional newsroom isn't on any cut list I've heard of. Most of my week is sitting with people on hospital waiting lists, and a chatbot that saves me twenty minutes on transcripts doesn't change that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing, and work on the radio stuff with Dev, our producer, who's offered to do practice sessions on Thursdays. I'd keep saving toward a house deposit with Priya, we put in about six hundred a month each. I'd keep using the transcript tool when it's handy, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. My worries in this picture are normal ones, like being bad at radio and house prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the budget's tight. What would happen if the newsroom did lose posts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last time there were cuts, they went for the late shift and sports, not health. And there are plenty of other newsrooms in the city, commercial radio, two websites, the daily paper. I'd be fine, just annoyed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your cushion like if something went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About ten months of pay in savings, most of it earmarked for the deposit. I'd rather not touch it, but it's there. Priya's a primary teacher, so between us there's always one steady wage.

say: I'd say newsrooms got **sold hype**, and reporting is still about ringing people and turning up.
I'd post a **told-you-so** on the team chat, gently.
think: Privately my job looks **about as safe** as a junior reporting job gets.
The **transcript tool** saves twenty minutes, but it doesn't touch the real work with patients.
do: Practise **radio delivery** on Thursdays with the producer, Dev.
Keep saving about **six hundred** a month toward a house deposit.
Keep using the **transcript tool** when it's handy.
feel: Pretty **calm**, with ordinary worries about radio nerves and **house prices**.
S0.quote: Most of my week is sitting with people on hospital waiting lists, and a chatbot that saves me twenty minutes on transcripts doesn't change that.
fieldNote: He sees his job as **people-facing**, which keeps him calm when AI adds little.
His cushion is **real**: ten months saved and a partner with a steady teaching job.
His only weak spot is **radio nerves**, and he's already working on it.

steps.text: Do Thursday radio practice sessions with the producer, Dev
Put six hundred a month toward the house deposit with Priya
Keep using the AI transcript tool for long interviews

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one bites. Writing and checking is a lot of the online side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say public money should go on journalists, not software licences. I'd say it at union meetings and probably online. If the public broadcaster saves money with AI, that money should go back into more reporters on the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing a cash-strapped public broadcaster cuts is the junior who writes up press releases, and that's mostly what I do on Mondays. The patient stories are safer, but they're slower and editors count output. I'm not the best writer on the desk yet. So I'd say my job shrinks, maybe to a part-time radio role, before it disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools properly, once I'd seen what the senior reporters were doing with them, so I'm not the one who refuses. I'd ask Martin for more time on original patient stories and less on press releases. I'd go to the union branch and push for a deal that any saving goes into reporting jobs. And we'd hold off on the house for a year, keep the deposit liquid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy going on worried. It's the first time I'd feel like my job is something that could be taken off me, rather than something I just need to get better at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off on the house. How did Priya feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be disappointed, we've been looking at two-bed places near her school. But she'd get it. She's the one who reads the bank statements, so she'd probably suggest it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the desk would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Saira, who does the overnight web shift. Her whole job is updating stories and writing up police statements, which is exactly what this card says goes first. She's got a little boy, too.

say: I'd say **public money** should pay for journalists, not software licences.
I'd argue any **AI savings** should go back into reporters on the ground.
think: Privately, the junior who **rewrites press releases** is the first post a tight budget cuts.
I expect my job to **shrink** to part-time radio work before it disappears.
do: Learn the **AI tools** properly once senior reporters show how they use them.
Ask Martin for **more patient stories** and fewer press release rewrites.
Delay the **house purchase** by a year and keep the deposit in cash.
feel: **Worried** for the first time that his job could be taken away, not just improved.
S1.quote: The first thing a cash-strapped public broadcaster cuts is the junior who writes up press releases, and that's mostly what I do on Mondays.
fieldNote: He's **steady**: he'd follow senior colleagues onto AI rather than lead or refuse.
He spots exactly **which part** of his week is most exposed.
His **politics** show up as wanting savings ploughed back into reporting jobs.

steps.text: Learn the newsroom's AI tools once senior reporters have tested them
Push the union branch to put AI savings into reporting jobs
Delay buying a two-bed flat with Priya by a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. That's quicker than a hospital waiting list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs emergency rules, like we'd do for a pandemic. Governments should be paying people's wages while they retrain, not leaving it to the market. I'd say that on air if they let me, and definitely at every union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job is gone. My work is nearly all thinking work, calls and writing, so it goes in 2028, not 2031. For the first time since we met, my girlfriend's teaching job would be the safe one and my journalism job the risky one. That's a weird thing to say about a seven-year-olds' classroom, but kids still need a person in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd stop the house hunt and keep everything in savings, ten months of pay could be stretched to fifteen if we lived on Priya's wage. I'd talk to the union about collective redundancy terms before the cuts land, not after. And I'd start looking at retraining into something hands-on, maybe something in health, since that gets a few more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly. It's the speed. Two years is one budget cycle at the public broadcaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually retrain in, if you had to pick now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've spent three years in hospitals, so probably something like healthcare assistant first, then maybe nursing. I'd want to see others doing it first, though. I'm not someone who jumps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Holidays, definitely, we were going to go walking in the mountains next summer. Then eating out. We're not big spenders anyway, so it's more about not making any big commitments.

say: I'd say we need **emergency rules**, the way we would in a pandemic.
Governments should pay **wages during retraining** instead of leaving it to the market.
think: Privately I think my job is **gone in 2028**, because it's nearly all thinking work.
My girlfriend's **teaching job** would become the safe one, which flips our whole plan.
do: Stop **house hunting** and keep all savings in cash.
Push the union for **redundancy terms** before cuts land.
Look at retraining as a **healthcare assistant** while hands-on work lasts longer.
feel: **Scared**, mostly by the speed: two years is one budget cycle.
S2.quote: For the first time since we met, my girlfriend's teaching job would be the safe one and my journalism job the risky one.
fieldNote: He sees clearly that **robots arriving later** makes hands-on health work a refuge for a while.
Even alarmed, he'd **wait to see others** retrain before jumping.
His cushion stretches to about **fifteen months** on his partner's wage.

steps.text: Keep all ten months of savings in an easy-access account
Push the union for collective redundancy terms before cuts
Look at healthcare assistant training at the local hospital
Stop house hunting and cancel next summer's mountain walking trip

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is still fast, but at least it's a plan's worth of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to build a proper safety net, so let's start now. I'd want my newsroom to report on it honestly, including on ourselves. I'd be pushing for a basic income pilot in our region, because I've seen what precarious work does to people's health.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give myself one year to see if the newsroom has a plan, and if it doesn't, I'd start a nursing degree at 29. AGI hits my writing in 2031, but nursing has the robots coming later, around 2034, and even then I think patients want a person. It's not the career I imagined. It might be a better one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd stay at work, learn the AI tools everyone else is using, and quietly volunteer a shift a month at the hospital to see if I could stand it. We'd still buy a smaller flat, because five years of Priya's pay plus my savings is enough for a small mortgage. Then I'd apply for the nursing course for the second year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. It's like knowing an exam date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you be worried about money during a nursing degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but less than most people. We'd have the flat and my savings would cover the gap for about three years if we're careful. I'm lucky, I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said patients want a person. What makes you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure, really, nobody is. But I've watched an old man hold a nurse's hand for twenty minutes before an operation. I'd bet a lot on that lasting longer than my web copy.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to build a safety net, so start now.
I'd push for a **basic income** pilot in the region.
think: Privately I'd give the newsroom **one year** to show a plan before leaving.
I'd likely start a **nursing degree** at 29, where robots arrive later and patients want people.
do: Learn the **AI tools** at work and volunteer a hospital shift monthly.
Buy a **smaller flat** with Priya using savings and her teaching wage.
Apply for a **nursing course** in the second year.
feel: **Anxious** but workable, like knowing an **exam date**.
S3.quote: I'd give myself one year to see if the newsroom has a plan, and if it doesn't, I'd start a nursing degree at 29.
fieldNote: Five years gives him a **staged plan**: test, then retrain into nursing.
His **health beat** gives him a real insight into which work keeps a human touch.
He admits **uncertainty** about whether patients will want people, but would still bet on it.

steps.text: Volunteer one hospital shift a month to test nursing
Learn the newsroom AI tools the rest of the desk uses
Buy a smaller flat with Priya on her teaching wage
Campaign for a regional basic income pilot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough to have a whole other career by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the chance to do it right: retraining funds, union deals, public money for local news. I'd write about it a lot, because it's a health story too. Insecure work makes people ill, and I'd keep making that point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've interviewed a hundred nurses about burnout, and I never once thought I'd end up asking one of them for advice on becoming one. With ten years, I'd have time to get properly good at journalism first and then move. I'd probably stay until about 2030 and then train, so I'm qualified well before the robots in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reporting, buy the flat with Priya next year as we planned, and keep saving. I'd use AI tools like everyone else for transcripts and research. Around 2029 I'd start talking seriously to nurses I know about training, then apply. I'd stay in the union the whole time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than scared. My own income looks safe for years, there's just a big change sitting on the horizon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your editor about the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for a few years. Martin's good, but you don't tell your boss you're leaving in 2030 when it's 2026. I'd tell Priya, and probably my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you're wrong and nursing gets automated too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have ten years of savings and two qualifications, which is more than most people. I'd rather be wrong in that direction than sit still.

say: I'd say this is the chance for **retraining funds**, union deals and public money for news.
I'd keep reporting that **insecure work** makes people ill.
think: Privately I'd get properly good at journalism, then **switch around 2030**.
Training as a **nurse** gets me qualified well before robots arrive in 2039.
do: Buy the **flat** with Priya next year as planned.
Use **AI tools** for transcripts and research like the rest of the desk.
Start talking to nurses about **training around 2029**.
feel: **Uneasy**, not scared: his income looks safe for years, with a big change on the horizon.
S4.quote: I've interviewed a hundred nurses about burnout, and I never once thought I'd end up asking one of them for advice on becoming one.
fieldNote: Ten years makes his **own income** feel safe, so worry drops to unease.
His plan is **the same as** five years, just slower and better funded.
He'd keep the plan **private from his editor** for years.

steps.text: Keep reporting on health at the regional newsroom until about 2030
Buy the flat with Priya next year as planned
Use AI tools for transcripts and background research
Ask nurse contacts about training routes around 2029

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My whole job is thinking work and two years is one budget cycle. What would help is paid retraining, so I could do a nursing course without burning the deposit, and a union deal that gives juniors decent redundancy terms, not just the people with twenty years in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what unions are actually for in all this. A union can't stop a machine, but a union can make sure the people it replaces don't get thrown out with nothing. That's what I'd want people to hear.

headlineQuote: A union can't stop a machine, but a union can make sure the people it replaces don't get thrown out with nothing.
portrait: Liam is a **27-year-old** health reporter at a public broadcaster's regional newsroom, still nervous on radio.
He uses **AI** now and then for transcripts and would follow colleagues before leading.
Ten months of savings and his girlfriend's **teaching job** give the household a steady base.
He moves from **calm** in the hype world to alarmed when AGI comes in two years.
With time, he'd plan a **switch to nursing**, drawn from years of interviewing patients.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his work is almost all thinking work and two years is one budget cycle.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** so a nursing course doesn't eat the house deposit.
A **union deal** giving juniors decent redundancy terms.
